posts.title: Is Tower Records Still Around? Online and in Japan
posts.excerpt: Tower Records is still around as an online store and a chain in Japan, but all 89 US stores closed after the 2006 bankruptcy auction.

posts.title: Who Owns eToys.com Now? Toys R Us Bought the Name
posts.excerpt: Toys R Us has owned eToys.com since February 2009, paying a reported $2.15 million. The original eToys died in 2001, two years after a $76 IPO pop.

posts.title: Broadcast.com: The $5.7 Billion Site Yahoo Shut Down
posts.excerpt: Yahoo bought Broadcast.com for $5.7 billion in 1999 and closed the service by 2002. The company had booked $22.4 million of revenue in 1998.

posts.title: EverQuest in 2026: The 1999 MMO That Still Runs
posts.excerpt: EverQuest is still active in 2026: Darkpaw Games runs the 1999 MMO, and a new server called Lethar opened on August 26, 2026.

posts.title: Is Angelfire Still Online? Lycos Closed It in 2026
posts.excerpt: Angelfire is not still online. Lycos took the free web host down on April 24, 2026, after a January outage and 30 days of notice.

posts.title: Are Heelys Still Sold in 2026? Who Owns Them Now
posts.excerpt: Heelys are still sold new in 2026, owned by BBC International, which paid $11 million for the brand in 2021. Peak year: 6.2 million pairs in 2006.

posts.title: Why Discovery Zone Failed and What's Left in 2026
posts.excerpt: Discovery Zone failed after two bankruptcies and closed for good by the end of 2001. One unaffiliated center still uses the name in 2026.

posts.title: How Many Rainforest Cafes Are Left? 16 in the US
posts.excerpt: Rainforest Cafe is down to 16 US restaurants in 11 states in 2026, from a peak of 59. Landry's owns it, and the Paris location closes in November.

posts.title: Who Owns Kinko's Now? FedEx Retired the Brand
posts.excerpt: Kinko's is gone in the US: FedEx bought it for $2.4 billion, then took an $891 million charge in 2008 to stop using the name.

posts.title: Is Toonami Still On TV in 2026? Yes, on Adult Swim
posts.excerpt: Toonami is still on TV in 2026: Adult Swim airs it Saturdays, midnight to 4 a.m. ET. Cartoon Network killed it in 2008 and a 2012 prank revived it.

posts.title: Why G4 TV Failed Twice: The 1,000-Viewer Collapse
posts.excerpt: G4 TV failed twice. Comcast unplugged the gaming channel on December 31, 2014, revived it in November 2021, and shut it down again in October 2022.

posts.title: Is Photobucket Still Around? Why Your Photos Vanished
posts.excerpt: Photobucket is still around in 2026, but only as paid storage: free accounts ended in June 2023 and plans now start at $5 a month for 1TB.

posts.title: Does Yahoo Messenger Still Exist? Why It Shut Down
posts.excerpt: Yahoo Messenger does not exist: Oath shut it down on July 17, 2018 after 20 years. Its replacement, Yahoo Together, lasted until April 4, 2019.

posts.title: Who Owns Game Informer Now? Gunzilla Games Does
posts.excerpt: Game Informer is owned by Gunzilla Games, which bought it in March 2025 after GameStop killed it in 2024. Issue 381 marks 35 years in print.

posts.title: How Many KB Toys Stores Are Left? Zero Since 2009
posts.excerpt: How many KB Toys stores are left? Zero. All 461 closed by February 9, 2009, and the brand now survives online and at a Comic-Con booth.

posts.title: Where Is FAO Schwarz Now? Inside Rockefeller Center
posts.excerpt: FAO Schwarz is still open, but not on Fifth Avenue. The flagship moved to 30 Rockefeller Plaza in 2018, and Nordstrom shops followed in 2026.

posts.title: Is Woolworth Still in Business? Only as Foot Locker
posts.excerpt: Woolworth is still in business, but only as Foot Locker: it renamed itself in 2001, four years after shutting all 400 US five-and-dime stores.

posts.title: Who Owns Sharper Image Now? No Stores Since 2008
posts.excerpt: Sharper Image is owned by ThreeSixty Group, which paid $100 million for the name in December 2016. No stores have existed since the 2008 collapse.

posts.title: Is the Disney Store Still Open? 21 Left in 2026
posts.excerpt: The Disney Store is still open, but only about 21 locations are left in North America in 2026, down from 747 stores at the 1999 peak.

posts.title: Where to Buy a Game Boy in 2026 and What to Pay
posts.excerpt: Buying a Game Boy in 2026 costs about $70 for a tested original, over $300 boxed. Check the LCD lines and battery terminals before you pay.

posts.title: Can You Still Get Dial-Up Internet? NetZero Does
posts.excerpt: Can you still get dial-up internet? Yes. NetZero, Juno and Microsoft's MSN all sell it in 2026, a year after AOL shut its dialer for good.

posts.title: How Many Sam Goody Stores Are Left? Exactly One
posts.excerpt: Exactly one Sam Goody store is left in 2026, at a mall in Medford, Oregon. Musicland closed 226 of them in a single month in 2006.

posts.title: When Did Netflix Stop Mailing DVDs? The Last Disc
posts.excerpt: Netflix stopped mailing DVDs on September 29, 2023, after 25 years and 5.2 billion discs. The last red envelope held a Blu-ray of True Grit.

posts.title: Is Columbia House Still Around? The 2026 Shutdown
posts.excerpt: Columbia House stops taking new orders after September 15, 2026, closing after 71 years. The club peaked in 1996 with 16 million members.

posts.title: Scan Old Photos and Negatives: DIY vs Mail-In Cost
posts.excerpt: Scan old photos at home or mail them out: a prepaid box of about 1,800 prints runs $145 in 2026, and 400 ppi is the resolution to use.

posts.title: Does Nokia Still Make Phones? Who Makes Them Now
posts.excerpt: Does Nokia still make phones? No. Nokia sold its handset business to Microsoft in 2013, and the last Nokia smartphones were pulled in January 2025.

posts.title: Who Owns Borders Now? The $13.9 Million Brand Sale
posts.excerpt: Borders closed its last US stores in September 2011. Barnes & Noble owns the name now, bought for $13.9 million with 48 million customer records.

posts.title: Is Hollywood Video Still Around? Every Store Closed
posts.excerpt: Hollywood Video is gone. Movie Gallery liquidated the last 1,900-plus US stores in 2010, and its late fees chased 3.3 million customers for years.

posts.title: Is Barnes and Noble Still Open? 720+ Stores in 2026
posts.excerpt: Barnes and Noble is still open and growing: more than 720 US stores in 2026, with 60 more planned. Elliott has owned the chain since 2019.

posts.title: Is an Anbernic Handheld Worth It for Game Boy?
posts.excerpt: An Anbernic handheld is worth it for Game Boy games if you bring your own files. Prices start under $60, but US shipping stopped in April 2025.

posts.title: Who Owns Claire's Now? The $140 Million Buyout
posts.excerpt: Claire's is owned by Ames Watson, which bought the chain out of bankruptcy in 2025 for about $140 million. Roughly 900 stores are still open.

posts.title: How Many Boston Market Locations Are Left in 2026?
posts.excerpt: Boston Market is down to about six listed locations in 2026, and only three answered the phone. It had 1,143 restaurants in 1998. Here is what closed them.

posts.title: Does Chuck E. Cheese Still Have Animatronics?
posts.excerpt: Chuck E. Cheese still has animatronics, but only in five US stores. Every other stage came out by the end of 2024, and the robots went to Kansas.

posts.title: Is GameStop Still in Business? 1,598 Stores Left
posts.excerpt: GameStop is still in business in 2026, but it closed 727 US stores in one year and ended January with 1,598 left. Games are now under 12% of sales.

posts.title: How to Run 90s PC Games on Windows 11 in 2026
posts.excerpt: Windows 11 is 64-bit only, so 90s PC games need help: DOSBox Staging, ScummVM or a GOG re-release. Two of the three cost nothing in 2026.

posts.title: Why Did Skype Shut Down? What Replaced It in 2025
posts.excerpt: Skype shut down on May 5, 2025 and Microsoft Teams Free replaced it. Skype Credit still works in Teams, but the old chats were deleted in 2026.

posts.title: Is Redbox Still Around? Why Kiosks Are Still There
posts.excerpt: Redbox is gone: its parent was liquidated in July 2024 and all 24,000 kiosks went dark. Thousands still stand because removal runs about $500 each.

posts.title: Dial-Up Sound Explained: What Each Screech Meant
posts.excerpt: The dial-up sound was two modems measuring a phone line: answer tone, capability menus, a 21-tone probe. AOL switched it off on September 30, 2025.

posts.title: Who Owns Yahoo Now? The $5 Billion Apollo Takeover
posts.excerpt: Yahoo is owned by Apollo Global Management, which paid about $5 billion in 2021. Verizon kept 10 percent. Microsoft once offered $44.6 billion.

posts.title: Sega Genesis Games in 2026: The Best Way to Play
posts.excerpt: The best way to play Sega Genesis games in 2026 is a used console and a flash cart, about $65 for the console, or $49.99 a year with no hardware.

posts.title: Is Habbo Hotel Still Around? The Pixel Hotel in 2026
posts.excerpt: Habbo Hotel is still online in 2026, run by Sulake and owned by Azerion, with 300 million registered accounts and a 2005 replica running next door.

posts.title: Does Yahoo Answers Still Exist? Why It Shut Down
posts.excerpt: Yahoo Answers does not still exist. It went read-only on April 20, 2021 and closed on May 4, 2021, 15 years after launch. Here is what survived.

posts.title: Betamax vs VHS: Why Sony Lost the First Format War
posts.excerpt: Betamax vs VHS came down to tape length, price and factories, not picture quality. Sony sold 18 million decks and made tapes until 2016.

posts.title: Who Owns Napster in 2026? Every Owner Since 2001
posts.excerpt: Napster is owned by Napster Corporation, formerly Infinite Reality, which paid $207 million in 2025 and killed the music service on January 1, 2026.

posts.title: How to Digitize VHS Tapes in 2026: DIY vs Legacybox
posts.excerpt: How to digitize VHS tapes in 2026: about $30 to $80 in capture gear at home, or $15 to $30 a tape by mail. Your tapes are past 25 years old.

posts.title: Who Was the AOL 'You've Got Mail' Voice? Elwood Edwards
posts.excerpt: Elwood Edwards recorded AOL's 'You've Got Mail' on a living room cassette in 1989 and was paid $200 once. He died in 2024, and AOL still plays it.

posts.title: Is Sega Still Making Games? Life After the Dreamcast
posts.excerpt: Is Sega still making games? Yes. Its games arm sold 326.6 billion yen worth last fiscal year, and Sonic 3 grossed 492.2 million dollars.

posts.title: Is RuneScape Still Popular in 2026? OSRS vs RS3
posts.excerpt: Is RuneScape still popular? Old School RuneScape peaked above 240,000 players at once in 2025, roughly eight times RuneScape 3. Here is who owns Jagex.

posts.title: Is MySpace Still Around? What Is Left of the Site
posts.excerpt: Is MySpace still around? Yes, myspace.com is online in 2026 and owned by Viant Technology. But a 2019 server migration erased 50 million songs.

posts.title: Is Kmart Still Open? The 3 Stores Left in 2026
posts.excerpt: Is Kmart still open in 2026? Yes, but only three stores are left: Miami, Guam and St. Thomas. It had 2,114 the day it filed for bankruptcy.

posts.title: Is CompUSA Still Around? What Happened to the Chain
posts.excerpt: Is CompUSA still around? No. The chain sold its last 103 stores in December 2007, and the brand was written off for $35.3 million in 2012.

posts.title: Windows 95 Startup Sound: Brian Eno's 3.25 Seconds
posts.excerpt: Brian Eno wrote the Windows 95 startup sound to a 3.25-second brief, made 84 versions, and did it on a Mac. The Library of Congress took it in 2025.

posts.title: Who Owns Sears Now, and How Many Stores Are Left?
posts.excerpt: Sears is owned by Eddie Lampert's Transformco and it is still trading. The last count found five full-line stores left, down from about 3,500.

posts.title: Who Owns Atari Now? The Brand That Refuses to Die
posts.excerpt: Atari is owned by Atari SA in Paris and run by Wade Rosen. The brand sold for $5 million in 1998 and booked about $65 million last year.

posts.title: Is Toys R Us Still in Business? What Survived 2018
posts.excerpt: Toys R Us closed all 735 US stores on June 29, 2018. The brand survived: WHP Global owns it, and 1,664 stores now trade in 35 countries.

posts.title: Is Palm Still a Company? From Pilot to a $349 Phone
posts.excerpt: Is Palm still a company? No. HP bought it for $1.2 billion in 2010, sold webOS to LG, and TCL has owned the dormant Palm brand since 2014.

posts.title: Is Netscape Still Around? What Happened After AOL
posts.excerpt: Is Netscape still around? The browser died in 2008, netscape.com redirects to AOL, and the trademark is still live under a new owner as of 2026.

posts.title: Is Blockbuster Still Open? The Last Store in 2026
posts.excerpt: Is Blockbuster still open? Yes, but only one store, in Bend, Oregon. Who owns the brand in 2026, how 9,000 stores became one, and what it sells.

posts.title: Does AOL Still Exist? What You Get for $10 a Month
posts.excerpt: Does AOL still exist? Yes. Italy's Bending Spoons bought it for about $1.5 billion in January 2026, and dial-up died on September 30, 2025.

posts.title: How Compaq Lost the PC Business It Helped Invent
posts.excerpt: Compaq went from a pie-shop sketch in 1982 to the world's biggest PC maker, then sold itself to HP for $25 billion. Here is what broke first.

posts.title: Why Iridium Failed: The $5 Billion Satellite Phone
posts.excerpt: Iridium put 66 satellites in orbit for about $5 billion, opened for business in 1998, and filed for bankruptcy nine months later. It sold for $25 million.

posts.title: The Beanie Babies Bubble: How a $5 Toy Went Bust
posts.excerpt: Beanie Babies were a $5 toy people traded like stocks in 1998. How Ty Inc. built the bubble, why it burst in 1999, and what the bears are worth now.

posts.title: Why the NSA Banned Furby: The 1998 Toy Craze Explained
posts.excerpt: Furby sold 1.8 million units in its first holiday season, hit $100 on the resale market, and got banned from NSA headquarters in January 1999. Here is why.

posts.title: What Happened to the Sega Channel, the Cable Service That Streamed Games in 1994
posts.excerpt: Before Xbox Game Pass, before the App Store, before broadband was even a word people used, Sega tried to deliver video games to your Genesis through your cable TV box. For a hot minute in the mid '90s, it almost worked.

posts.title: What Happened to HyperCard, the Apple Software That Quietly Invented the Web
posts.excerpt: In 1987 Apple shipped a program with every Macintosh that let anyone build clickable, multimedia documents with no programming experience required. It was called HyperCard, and almost everything you do on the internet today is a copy of it.

posts.title: Why the Sega 32X Failed: The $159.99 Add-On Flop
posts.excerpt: The Sega 32X launched November 21, 1994 at $159.99, sold about 665,000 units, shipped 40 games, and was cleared out at $19.95 before dying in 1996.

posts.title: The First Banner Ad: How One Click on October 27, 1994 Built the Modern Web
posts.excerpt: On October 27, 1994, an AT&T banner ad ran on HotWired with a 44 percent click-through rate. Three decades later, every website you use is shaped by what happened that day.

posts.title: What Happened to the Game Genie, the $50 Cheat Device That Beat Nintendo in Court
posts.excerpt: Galoob's Game Genie sat between a NES cartridge and the console and lied about how many lives Mario had. Nintendo sued. Galoob won. A whole modding generation was born from a $50 plastic sleeve and a six-letter code.

posts.title: What Happened to Geocaching, the GPS Treasure Hunt That Started With a Bucket and a Can of Beans
posts.excerpt: When the US military stopped degrading civilian GPS signals on May 1, 2000, a hobbyist in Oregon hid a bucket in the woods the next day. That bucket became geocaching, a 3-million-cache, 191-country platform with a 25-year run.

posts.title: What Happened to the Nintendo Power Glove: 1989's Worst Best Toy
posts.excerpt: Mattel's Power Glove promised motion-controlled NES gaming in 1989. It barely worked, only two games supported it, and somehow it became one of the most beloved failures in video game history.

posts.title: What Happened to theGlobe.com: The Biggest IPO Pop in History
posts.excerpt: In 1998 two Cornell undergrads took theGlobe.com public and watched the stock pop 606 percent on day one. It remains the largest first-day gain in IPO history. Here's the full story of how it happened and why it collapsed.

posts.title: What Happened to the Atari Lynx, the Color Handheld That Lost to Game Boy
posts.excerpt: In 1989, the Atari Lynx had a backlit color screen, hardware sprite scaling, and 8-player networking. It got crushed by a $90 gray brick called the Game Boy. Here is exactly why.

posts.title: What Happened to Excite, the Search Engine That Turned Down Google for $750,000
posts.excerpt: In 1999, Excite was worth $35 billion and had the chance to buy Google for $750,000. CEO George Bell said no. The full story is more complicated, and a lot more interesting, than the punchline suggests.

posts.title: What Happened to the TurboGrafx-16, NEC's Forgotten 16-Bit Console
posts.excerpt: It was the king of Japan, the third option in America, and the console that invented half the things we now take for granted. Then it disappeared.

posts.title: What Happened to PointCast and the 1990s Push Technology Boom
posts.excerpt: In 1997, News Corporation offered $450 million for a company that delivered headlines through a screensaver. Two years later it sold for $7 million. The full story of push technology's rise and collapse.

posts.title: How the Nintendo NES Saved Video Games After the 1983 Crash
posts.excerpt: In 1985, American retailers had given up on video games. Then a Japanese toy company shipped a gray plastic box with a robot, called it an entertainment system, and resurrected an entire industry. This is the full story of how the NES pulled gaming back from the dead.

posts.title: What Happened to Standalone GPS Devices: TomTom and the Smartphone Killer
posts.excerpt: In 2008, the world bought 42 million standalone GPS devices. By 2014, the category was effectively dead. The story of how a free Android feature, a Cold War satellite system, and an $11 billion map data war ended an entire consumer electronics market.

posts.title: What Happened to TechTV and The Screen Savers Channel
posts.excerpt: ZDTV launched in 1998. Comcast killed it in less than a year after the 2004 G4 merger. Here is how a cable channel built for nerds disappeared, and where its hosts went.

posts.title: What Happened to Wine.com and the Internet Wine Wars
posts.excerpt: Three companies burned through more than $200M trying to sell wine online between 1995 and 2001. The smallest one ended up owning the Wine.com domain.

posts.title: What Happened to the Nokia 3310, the Phone That Refused to Die
posts.excerpt: Nokia's 3310 sold 126 million units, became an internet meme for being indestructible, and got resurrected from the grave in 2017. Here is the full story of how a small Finnish company built a phone so good it accidentally turned into a cultural symbol.

posts.title: What Happened to NCSA Mosaic, the Browser That Built the World Wide Web
posts.excerpt: Before Netscape, before Internet Explorer, there was Mosaic. The browser two students built at a public university in 1993 became the front door to the early web, then quietly disappeared while reshaping the next thirty years of the internet.

posts.title: What Happened to the Sega CD, the Add-On That Promised Gaming's Future
posts.excerpt: Sega bolted a CD-ROM drive onto the Genesis, charged $299, and promised the future of video games. Here is the messy, fascinating story of how it all went sideways.

posts.title: What Happened to Prodigy, the Online Service That Beat AOL to America
posts.excerpt: Before AOL, before the web, two of the biggest companies in America spent over a billion dollars trying to teach the country how to go online. Prodigy got there first, then lost everything.

posts.title: What Happened to the 3DO, the $700 Console That Bombed
posts.excerpt: In 1993, a console hit shelves at $699.99 and promised to be the VHS of gaming. Instead, the 3DO became one of the most spectacular flops in video game history. Here is the full story.

posts.title: What Happened to Microsoft Bob, the Friendly Interface That Failed
posts.excerpt: In 1995, Microsoft tried to replace the desktop with a cartoon house full of talking pets. It sold around 58,000 copies and got pulled from shelves within a year. Here is what really happened.

posts.title: What Happened to the Sony Discman, the CD Player That Changed Music
posts.excerpt: The Sony Discman made music portable on compact disc for the first time. Here is the full story of how it changed everything, then quietly disappeared.

posts.title: What Happened to Xanga, the Blog Platform Before Blogging Was Cool
posts.excerpt: Xanga had 27 million users before most people knew what a blog was. Then it vanished. The real story involves a $1 million FTC fine, a failed crowdfunding campaign, and the rise of Facebook.

posts.title: What Happened to StarCraft, the Game That Invented Esports
posts.excerpt: How a real-time strategy game from 1998 accidentally built a billion-dollar esports industry, turned South Korean teenagers into national celebrities, and changed competitive gaming forever.

posts.title: What Happened to Kodak, the Company That Invented the Digital Camera Then Chose to Ignore It
posts.excerpt: Kodak controlled 90% of the American film market, employed over 145,000 people, and invented the digital camera in 1975. Then it spent three decades pretending digital photography wasn't coming.

posts.title: What Happened to the Virtual Boy, Nintendo's Most Embarrassing Failure
posts.excerpt: Nintendo's legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi created the Game Boy. Then he created the Virtual Boy, which sold 770,000 units and gave everyone a headache.

posts.title: What Happened to the Segway, the Invention That Was Supposed to Change the World
posts.excerpt: Investors predicted a billion dollars in first-year sales. The Segway sold roughly 140,000 units across its entire twenty-year lifetime.

posts.title: What Happened to the Game Boy, Nintendo's Unbreakable Handheld
posts.excerpt: How a monochrome brick with an 8-bit processor outlasted every competitor with color screens and better specs, sold 118 million units, and accidentally created the template for portable gaming.

posts.title: How the iMac G3 Saved Apple and Killed the Beige Box Forever
posts.excerpt: In 1997, Apple was losing $878 million a year and Michael Dell said they should shut it down. Then a translucent blue computer changed the entire industry.

posts.title: What Happened to Counter-Strike, the Mod That Became Bigger Than the Game
posts.excerpt: Two modders, an ICQ chat, and a Half-Life SDK turned into over 50 million copies sold and the birth of competitive PC gaming as we know it.

posts.title: What Happened to Tumblr, the Platform Yahoo Bought for a Billion and Sold for Pennies
posts.excerpt: Yahoo paid $1.1 billion for Tumblr in 2013. Six years later, Verizon sold it to Automattic for $3 million. Here's the full story of how a culture platform got killed by the companies that owned it.

posts.title: What Happened to Arcades: The Rise, Fall, and Unlikely Return of Quarter-Powered Gaming
posts.excerpt: In 1982, arcades earned more than Hollywood and the music industry combined. Then they vanished. Here's the complete story of what happened to arcades, from the golden age to the modern revival.

posts.title: What Happened to LiveJournal, the Platform That Invented Modern Blogging
posts.excerpt: LiveJournal had 18 million users and invented friends lists, access controls, and communities years before Facebook existed. Then its servers moved to Russia overnight.

posts.title: What Happened to Quake, the Game That Invented Online FPS
posts.excerpt: In 1996, id Software released a game that didn't just push graphics forward. It rewired how millions of people played together, competed, and thought about what a video game could be.

posts.title: What Happened to WebTV, the Box That Promised Internet for Everyone
posts.excerpt: In 1996, three former Apple engineers built a $325 box that let people browse the web on their televisions. Microsoft paid $425 million for it. By 2013, it was gone.

posts.title: What Happened to 3dfx? The Graphics Card That Ruled the '90s
posts.excerpt: It dominated the late 1990s with an iron fist, commanded 80% of the 3D graphics market, and fundamentally changed what PC gaming could be. Then in just a few years, it was gone.

posts.title: What Happened to Flickr, the Photo Site Yahoo Left to Die
posts.excerpt: Flickr once hosted nearly 2 billion photos and defined photo-sharing for a generation. Then Yahoo acquired it, removed the features that made it special, and left it to rot while Instagram ate its lunch.

posts.title: What Happened to Oregon Trail, the Game That Taught America to Die of Dysentery
posts.excerpt: Created in two weeks on a teletype by three student teachers in 1971, Oregon Trail became the most successful educational game ever made, selling 65 million copies before corporate acquisitions scattered its legacy.

posts.title: What Happened to GoldenEye 007, the Game That Proved FPS Could Work on Console
posts.excerpt: Built by ten first-time developers at a rural British studio, GoldenEye 007 sold 8 million copies and defined console multiplayer for a generation before licensing disputes made it nearly impossible to play for two decades.

posts.title: What Happened to IRC, the Chat Protocol That Built the Internet
posts.excerpt: Created in 1988 by a Finnish computer science student, IRC kept the internet connected during the Gulf War and became home to millions of users. But Discord and Slack made it obsolete.

posts.title: Is There a New Tony Hawk Game? The Series in 2026
posts.excerpt: No new Tony Hawk game is announced for 2026. The last one was Pro Skater 3 + 4 in July 2025, and its studio cut up to 90 jobs in April 2026.

posts.title: What Happened to the Sega Game Gear, the Handheld That Deserved Better
posts.excerpt: The Sega Game Gear had superior hardware, full color graphics, and backlit brilliance. So why did it lose to the Game Boy? Discover the tragic tale of ambitious hardware sabotaged by battery life and Sega's own chaos.

posts.title: What Happened to Eudora, the Email Client That Taught the Internet to Write
posts.excerpt: Eudora dominated email in the 1990s with 18 million users and dominated revenue. Gmail and webmail killed desktop email clients. Here's how the world's most popular email software disappeared.

posts.title: What Happened to SimCity and How EA Destroyed It
posts.excerpt: From Will Wright’s revolutionary city builder to EA’s catastrophic always-online launch, the rise and fall of SimCity is a cautionary tale about corporate mismanagement.

posts.title: What Happened to RollerCoaster Tycoon, Built by One Man in Assembly
posts.excerpt: Chris Sawyer wrote 99% of RollerCoaster Tycoon in assembly language, alone, and earned $30 million. Then the franchise left his hands.

posts.title: What Happened to Newgrounds, the Internet Before YouTube
posts.excerpt: From a kid's Neo Geo fanzine to the birthplace of internet animation. How Newgrounds built the creative web, survived the death of Flash, and keeps going.

posts.title: What Happened to BonziBuddy, the Internet's Friendliest Spyware
posts.excerpt: The purple gorilla that harvested your data. How BonziBuddy went from desktop companion to FTC settlement, and what it reveals about early internet trust.

posts.title: The Original Sims: How a Virtual Dollhouse Became the Best-Selling PC Game Ever
posts.excerpt: Will Wright pitched it as an architecture sim. EA almost killed it. Then it outsold every PC game in history and changed who we think of as a gamer.

posts.title: What Happened to Polaroid, the Camera That Died and Came Back
posts.excerpt: Polaroid peaked at $3 billion in revenue, went bankrupt twice, and was rescued by a group of enthusiasts who bought the last factory on Earth for $3.1 million.

posts.title: What Happened to Iomega Zip Drives and the Click of Death
posts.excerpt: The Zip drive made 100MB feel infinite, turned Iomega into a $7 billion company, and then a manufacturing defect brought it all crashing down.

posts.title: What Happened to Kazaa and the P2P Wars After Napster
posts.excerpt: Kazaa became the most downloaded software on Earth, survived where Napster couldn't, and still lost everything. The full story of the P2P wars.

posts.title: What Happened to Club Penguin, Disney's Accidental MMO
posts.excerpt: How three guys in Kelowna, BC built a virtual world that captured 200 million kids, sold to Disney for $350 million, and then vanished entirely.

posts.title: What Happened to MiniDisc, Sony's Forgotten Music Format
posts.excerpt: Sony spent billions building the perfect portable music format. It conquered Japan, flopped everywhere else, and now Gen Z is collecting them on TikTok.

posts.title: What Happened to Screensavers: Flying Toasters, 3D Pipes, and Doing Nothing
posts.excerpt: From a $30 million software company selling animated toasters to a forgotten Windows setting nobody touches, screensavers had one of the strangest rises and falls in tech history.

posts.title: What Happened to Clippy, the Paperclip Everyone Loved to Hate
posts.excerpt: Microsoft spent millions on user research, hired Stanford psychologists, tested 250 character designs, and somehow still created the most universally despised software feature of the 1990s.

posts.title: The Night Windows 95 Launched and Changed Everything
posts.excerpt: On August 24, 1995, people lined up at midnight to buy an operating system. Microsoft spent $300 million to make sure they did.

posts.title: What Happened to Commodore, the Company That Won and Lost
posts.excerpt: Commodore sold more home computers than anyone in history. Then its own executives drove it into the ground. Here is how it all fell apart.

posts.title: What Happened to Neopets, the Virtual World That Raised a Generation
posts.excerpt: From 150 million accounts and $160 million acquisitions to corporate neglect and a management buyout. The full story of how Neopets rose, fell, and tried to come back.

posts.title: How Doom Changed Everything About PC Gaming and the Internet
posts.excerpt: On December 10, 1993, five people in a Texas office uploaded a file that crashed a university network and generated $100,000 a day. The full story of how Doom rewrote the rules.

posts.title: What Happened to the Atari Jaguar? The Console That Killed Atari
posts.excerpt: Atari bet everything on a '64-bit' console with a phone keypad controller and 63 games. It sold fewer units than some accessories.

posts.title: What Happened to WordPerfect? The Software Microsoft Had to Kill Twice
posts.excerpt: WordPerfect once held 85% of the DOS word processor market and earned $700 million a year. Then Windows happened.

posts.title: What Happened to Creative Labs and the Sound Blaster?
posts.excerpt: The Sound Blaster didn't just give PCs a voice. It made them scream, sing, and explode. Then the world moved on.

posts.title: What Happened to Lycos, the Search Engine Worth $12 Billion?
posts.excerpt: Lycos went from Carnegie Mellon research project to the most visited site on the internet. Then it was sold for $36 million.

posts.title: What Happened to HD DVD? The Format War That Cost Toshiba Everything
posts.excerpt: Toshiba bet everything on HD DVD and lost to Blu-ray in a brutal two-year format war. Here's the full story of how Sony, the PS3, and one studio's decision ended it all.

posts.title: What Happened to Lotus 1-2-3? The Spreadsheet That Built the PC Industry
posts.excerpt: Lotus 1-2-3 was the original killer app, the reason businesses bought PCs. Then Microsoft Excel came along, and Lotus made one catastrophic strategic mistake.

posts.title: The iPod Wasn't the First MP3 Player. Here's Why It Won.
posts.excerpt: The Diamond Rio and Creative Nomad existed first. But Apple's iPod, with its scroll wheel and iTunes integration, became the device that changed how 450 million people listened to music.

posts.title: What Happened to Craigslist? The Ugliest Website Worth Billions
posts.excerpt: Craig Newmark's 1995 email list became a $1 billion business with 50 employees, killed the newspaper classified industry, and then quietly started shrinking. The site still looks the same.

posts.title: What Happened to the Nintendo Wii? The Console That Made Your Grandma a Gamer
posts.excerpt: Nintendo bet everything on a motion-controlled console with last-gen graphics. It sold 101 million units and changed gaming forever. Then the magic faded.

posts.title: Do They Still Make Netbooks? Why the Eee PC Died
posts.excerpt: No. Netbooks peaked at 38.8 million units in 2010 and died in 2012. Chromebooks under $200 and cheap Windows laptops replaced them.

posts.title: The PS2 Sold 160 Million Units. Nothing Has Topped It.
posts.excerpt: The PlayStation 2 outsold every competitor combined, doubled as the world's cheapest DVD player, and stayed in production for thirteen years. Here is how Sony built the most dominant console ever made.

posts.title: What Happened to CompuServe? The Online World Before the Web
posts.excerpt: CompuServe invented the GIF, pioneered online chat, and had three million subscribers before most people knew what a modem was. Then the open web made it obsolete overnight.

posts.title: What Happened to Gateway? The Cow Box Computer Company
posts.excerpt: Gateway 2000 started on a cattle ranch in Iowa with a $10,000 loan and turned cow-spotted boxes into the most recognizable brand in personal computing. Then it all fell apart.

posts.title: What Happened to Boo.com? The $135M Fashion Dot-Com Flop
posts.excerpt: Boo.com raised $135 million to sell designer fashion online, launched in 18 countries at once, and collapsed in six months. The concept was right. The timing was catastrophically wrong.

posts.title: Motorola Razr V3: 130 Million Sold, No Signal Left
posts.excerpt: The Motorola Razr V3 sold 130 million units, and since August 3, 2026 it cannot make a call in the US. What one costs second-hand now.

posts.title: Google Reader Is Gone and the Internet Never Recovered
posts.excerpt: Google Reader launched in 2005 as a 20% time project and became the internet's essential reading tool. Then Google killed it to push Google+, and we all moved to algorithmic feeds.

posts.title: What Happened to the Nokia N-Gage? The Gaming Phone That Became a Punchline
posts.excerpt: Nokia spent hundreds of millions trying to merge phones and gaming consoles into one device. The result was a $299 taco-shaped punchline that sold 3 million units instead of the projected 6 million, got outsold 100-to-1 by the Game Boy Advance, and accidentally predicted the future of mobile gaming.

posts.title: What Happened to Excite@Home? The $35 Billion Broadband Bet
posts.excerpt: In 1999, Excite@Home had a $35 billion market cap, 4.1 million broadband subscribers, and a vision for the high-speed internet future. By 2001, the stock had crashed from $128 to $1, the company filed for bankruptcy, and millions of Americans nearly lost their internet access overnight.

posts.title: What Happened to the Sega Saturn? The Console That Self-Destructed at Launch
posts.excerpt: Sega surprise-launched the Saturn at E3 1995 for $399, alienated every major retailer, and watched Sony destroy them with a single word: $299. The full story of gaming's most spectacular self-own.

posts.title: Why the Apple Newton Failed and What It Costs Now
posts.excerpt: Apple sold about 50,000 Newton MessagePads in three months, then killed the line in 1998. Why it failed, and what a MessagePad sells for now.

posts.title: What Happened to the Original Xbox? Microsoft's $4 Billion Bet on Gaming
posts.excerpt: Four engineers, a gutted Dell laptop, and a plan to trick Bill Gates into building a gaming console. The original Xbox was never supposed to exist.

posts.title: The AOL-Time Warner Merger: The Worst Deal in Corporate History
posts.excerpt: In January 2000, AOL bought Time Warner for $182 billion. Within three years, the combined company posted the largest annual loss ever recorded. Here is how it fell apart.

posts.title: The Golden Age of LAN Parties: When Gaming Meant Hauling Your PC Across Town
posts.excerpt: Before broadband killed the necessity and online gaming became the default, there was an era when playing multiplayer meant loading your 50-pound CRT monitor into your car and driving across town.

posts.title: What Happened to Kozmo.com? The Delivery App That Existed Before Your Phone Did
posts.excerpt: Kozmo.com raised $280 million promising free one-hour delivery of DVDs and snacks in 1998. It collapsed in 2001. Twenty years later, DoorDash proved the founders were right all along.

posts.title: What Happened to Circuit City? The Store That Fired Its Way to Death
posts.excerpt: Circuit City was once the biggest electronics retailer in America. Then it fired 3,400 of its best employees, and everything fell apart.

posts.title: How Amazon Survived the Dot-Com Crash (When Thousands Didn't)
posts.excerpt: Amazon's stock fell 94% during the dot-com bust. The company was months from running out of cash. Here is why it survived when nearly everyone else didn't.

posts.title: Is the PSP Still Supported? Sony's Handheld in 2026
posts.excerpt: The PSP is not supported in 2026. Sony sold more than 76.4 million, closed the PSP store in 2021, and PS3 and Vita sales end in July 2027.

posts.title: What Happened to Webvan? The Grocery Startup That Burned $800M
posts.excerpt: Webvan promised to revolutionize grocery shopping with 30-minute delivery windows and massive automated warehouses. Instead, it became the poster child for dot-com excess, burning through $800 million before collapsing in 2001. But was the idea really wrong, or just impossibly early?

posts.title: Why the Nintendo GameCube Lost the Console War
posts.excerpt: The Nintendo GameCube sold 21.74 million units to the PlayStation 2's 155 million and died in 2007. Its games returned on Switch 2 in June 2025.

posts.title: Is eBay Still Around in 2026? 135 Million Buyers
posts.excerpt: eBay is still around in 2026: a public Nasdaq company with 135 million buyers and $79.6 billion sold in 2025. It started with a broken laser pointer.

posts.title: Is RadioShack Still in Business? 2026 Store Count
posts.excerpt: Is RadioShack still in business? Yes, as a brand. The US chain died in the 2017 bankruptcy, and an El Salvador group has owned the name since 2023.

posts.title: Is Friendster Still Around? It Came Back in 2026
posts.excerpt: Friendster deleted every profile in 2011 and shut down in 2015, but the name relaunched in April 2026 as an app with no ads and no algorithm.

posts.title: Is Fry's Electronics Still Around? All 31 Stores Closed
posts.excerpt: Fry's Electronics is gone. All 31 remaining stores closed on February 24, 2021, with no bankruptcy filing and no farewell sale. Here is what is left.

posts.title: Does AltaVista Still Exist? Yahoo Closed It in 2013
posts.excerpt: AltaVista no longer exists: Yahoo closed the search engine on July 8, 2013. Apollo-owned Yahoo still holds the domain that sold for $140 million in 2003.

posts.title: Who Owns LimeWire Now? BabyDoge Bought It in 2026
posts.excerpt: LimeWire's file sharing died by court order in October 2010. The brand survived: BabyDoge bought it in September 2026, 8 million users and all.

posts.title: Is ICQ Still Around? VK Shut It Down in June 2024
posts.excerpt: ICQ shut down on June 26, 2024 after 28 years, and VK still owns the name. Free NINA servers now run ICQ 2000 through ICQ 8 clients.

posts.title: Does Ask Jeeves Still Exist? Ask.com Closed in 2026
posts.excerpt: Ask Jeeves became Ask.com, lost the butler in 2006, quit building its own search engine in 2010, and closed for good on May 1, 2026.

posts.title: Is TiVo Still Around in 2026? Yes, but Not the DVR
posts.excerpt: TiVo still exists in 2026 as smart TV software owned by Xperi, but it stopped selling DVR hardware on October 1, 2025, after 26 years.

posts.title: Is BlackBerry Still in Business? Yes, but No Phones
posts.excerpt: BlackBerry still exists, but it has not made a phone since 2016. It earned $549.1 million in fiscal 2026 from car software and secure messaging.

posts.title: Is Digg Still Around in 2026? Yes, as an AI Site
posts.excerpt: Digg still exists in 2026, but as an AI news aggregator run by Kevin Rose, not a Reddit rival. The relaunched app shut down on March 14, 2026.

posts.title: Is Second Life Still Around in 2026? Yes, 23 Years Later
posts.excerpt: Second Life is still running in 2026, 23 years after launch, with daily concurrency in the mid-30,000s and an economy near $650 million a year.

posts.title: Are Tamagotchis Still Made in 2026? Yes, by Bandai
posts.excerpt: Tamagotchi is still made by Bandai in 2026. Shipments passed 100 million in July 2025, new models cost $44.99, and 1997 originals fetch $40 to $50.

posts.title: Who Owns MTV Now, and Does It Still Play Music?
posts.excerpt: MTV is still on the air in 2026 and owned by Paramount Skydance, but its last five music-only channels went dark on December 31, 2025.

posts.title: Is Encarta Still Available? Why Microsoft Killed It
posts.excerpt: Microsoft Encarta is gone: disc sales ended in June 2009 and MSN Encarta closed October 31, 2009. What replaced it, and how to run it now.

posts.title: Is RealPlayer Still Around? Yes, Free From Real.com
posts.excerpt: RealPlayer still exists: RealNetworks shipped version 25 in 2026 and still gives it away free, with Plus at $39.99. It sells computer vision now.

posts.title: How MySpace Lost to Facebook and Sold for $35M
posts.excerpt: MySpace lost to Facebook after News Corporation tied the site to a $900 million Google ad deal. It sold for $35 million in June 2011.

posts.title: Is Google Glass Still Around? Discontinued in 2023
posts.excerpt: Google Glass is discontinued: sales ended March 15, 2023 and support that September. What the $1,500 headset was, and what Google sells now.

posts.title: Is the Microsoft Zune Still Around? Why It Failed
posts.excerpt: Microsoft Zune hardware died in 2011 and its services in 2015. Here is why it lost to the iPod, and what a used Zune HD costs in 2026.

posts.title: Is Adobe Flash Still Around? Flash Player in 2026
posts.excerpt: Adobe Flash Player died on December 31, 2020, but Flash is not fully gone: China still ships version 34 and over 200,000 games survive.

posts.title: Is Winamp Still Around in 2026? Yes, and It Works
posts.excerpt: Winamp still exists in 2026: Winamp Group owns it, and the free 5.9.2 player runs on Windows 11. A Deezer-powered version lands in 2027.

posts.title: Why Pets.com Failed and Where the Sock Puppet Went
posts.excerpt: Pets.com sold pet food below cost, IPO'd at $11 in February 2000 and shut its store that November. PetSmart owns the domain; the sock puppet outlived it.

posts.title: Why Google+ Failed and When Google Shut It Down
posts.excerpt: Google+ shut down on April 2, 2019 and Google Currents followed in 2023. Here is why a $585 million social network sat empty.

posts.title: Why Sega Stopped Making Consoles After Dreamcast
posts.excerpt: Sega stopped making consoles on January 31, 2001, after the Dreamcast sold 9.13 million units. It has not built one since, and still will not.

posts.title: Palm Pilot Explained: The PDA That Phones Replaced
posts.excerpt: The Palm Pilot sold a million units in 18 months, then lost to the smartphone. Palm shipped its last handhelds in October 2005.

posts.title: Who Owns MapQuest Now? System1 and the 2026 Surge
posts.excerpt: MapQuest is still around in 2026, owned by ad tech firm System1 since 2019. Google Maps only passed it in January 2009, by 700,000 users.

posts.title: Does Hotmail Still Exist? Outlook.com Runs It Now
posts.excerpt: Hotmail still exists. Microsoft retired the name in May 2013 and moved 300 million accounts to Outlook.com, where old addresses still work.

posts.title: Does GeoCities Still Exist? Where the Pages Went
posts.excerpt: GeoCities does not still exist. Yahoo deleted it on October 26, 2009, taking about 38 million pages. Archive Team saved 641 GB of them.

posts.title: Is MSN Messenger Still Around? Yes, on Escargot
posts.excerpt: MSN Messenger died in 2013 and Skype, the thing that replaced it, died in 2025. A free fan server called Escargot still runs it in 2026.

posts.title: Was Apple Really 90 Days From Bankruptcy in 1997?
posts.excerpt: Apple lost $1.04 billion in fiscal 1997 and Steve Jobs called it 90 days from insolvent. Microsoft's $150 million check landed on August 6, 1997.

posts.title: Is AIM Still Around? AOL Instant Messenger in 2026
posts.excerpt: Is AIM still around? No. AOL Instant Messenger shut down on December 15, 2017, and hobby servers are now the only way to sign on.

posts.title: Why Netscape Navigator Lost to Internet Explorer
posts.excerpt: Netscape Navigator lost to Internet Explorer because Microsoft gave IE away free and wired it into Windows. Navigator led 51% to 40% in 1997, then fell.

posts.title: Windows XP Bliss Wallpaper: Where the Hill Is Now
posts.excerpt: The Windows XP Bliss wallpaper hill is real, on private land off Fremont Drive in Sonoma County, and it turned green again on 18 February 2026.

posts.title: Y2K Explained: What Really Broke on January 1, 2000
posts.excerpt: The Y2K bug was real and the US spent about $100 billion killing it. Here is what still broke on January 1, 2000, from spy satellites to slot machines.

posts.title: Did Napster Kill the Music Industry? The 2026 Math
posts.excerpt: Napster did not kill the music industry. US revenue fell from $14.6 billion in 1999 to $8.5 billion in 2009, then hit a record $11.5 billion in 2025.

posts.title: What Is $1,000 From 1999 Worth in 2026 Dollars?
posts.excerpt: $1,000 from 1999 is worth about $2,000 in 2026. That is two weeks of a family health premium now, and it no longer buys the average PC.

posts.title: 90s Tech Prices in 2026 Dollars: Full 40-Item Table
posts.excerpt: A PlayStation cost $299 in 1995, or $655 in 2026 dollars. Forty sourced launch prices for 90s and early-2000s tech, adjusted with CPI-U.

posts.title: 90s Websites Still Online in 2026: 5 That Survived
posts.excerpt: Yes, 90s websites are still online in 2026: the 1996 Space Jam site lives at spacejam.com/1996 and info.cern.ch has run since 1991.

posts.title: Dial-Up Speed vs 2026 Internet: How Slow Was 56k?
posts.excerpt: Dial-up speed topped out at 53.3 kbit/s, about 1,876 times slower than the 100 Mbps broadband floor. AOL quit dial-up on September 30, 2025.

posts.title: What Was the First Thing Sold Online? PizzaNet vs a CD
posts.excerpt: The first thing sold online was not a pizza. PizzaNet took orders in August 1994, eleven days after a Sting CD sold for $12.48.

posts.title: Did Blockbuster Turn Down Netflix for $50 Million?
posts.excerpt: Blockbuster did turn down Netflix for $50 million in 2000. Netflix booked $45.2 billion in 2025 revenue; EchoStar now owns the Blockbuster name.

posts.title: Did Yahoo Turn Down Google for $1 Million in 1998?
posts.excerpt: Yahoo never bought Google and Google never bought Yahoo. The $1 million story is thinly sourced, and the real offer in 2002 was $3 billion.

posts.title: Microsoft Tried to Buy Nintendo and Got Laughed At
posts.excerpt: Microsoft tried to buy Nintendo in 1999 and spent an hour being laughed at. The letter survives, and the Xbox shipped two years later.
